reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A benign inherited disorder of calcium sensing that causes lifelong, usually asymptomatic, mild hypercalcaemia
The defining feature is hypercalcaemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion, reflected in a low calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio
PTH is typically normal or only mildly elevated despite the raised calcium, mimicking mild primary hyperparathyroidism
The calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (usually below 0.01) is the key test distinguishing it from primary hyperparathyroidism, where renal calcium handling is not conserved
It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, most often from inactivating mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor, so a family history of hypercalcaemia is common
Because the condition is benign, recognising it prevents unnecessary parathyroid surgery, which does not correct the abnormality
Homozygous or biallelic mutations cause neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism, a very different and life-threatening presentation
Confirmation of the diagnosis may involve genetic testing and screening of relatives
reference.pathophysiology: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is most commonly due to heterozygous inactivating mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) expressed on parathyroid cells and renal tubules. Reduced receptor sensitivity resets the threshold at which extracellular calcium suppresses PTH secretion, so the parathyroid glands perceive a normal calcium level as low and maintain PTH output despite hypercalcaemia. In the kidney, blunted CaSR signalling enhances tubular calcium reabsorption, producing the characteristic low urinary calcium excretion. The net result is stable, mild hypercalcaemia with preserved or slightly high PTH and avid renal calcium conservation. Related variants involve other components of calcium-sensing signalling.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium (corrected or ionised) and PTH
24-hour urinary calcium and the calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio
Serum magnesium (often high-normal or mildly elevated)
Vitamin D status and renal function to exclude alternative causes
Genetic testing of the calcium-sensing receptor and related genes
Family screening with serum calcium measurement
redFlags: Neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism in a newborn (biallelic disease) presenting with marked hypercalcaemia and requiring urgent intervention
Symptoms or biochemistry suggesting an alternative and more serious cause of hypercalcaemia such as malignancy
Unnecessary parathyroidectomy being planned for what is a benign condition
reference.prognosis: The heterozygous form is benign with an excellent prognosis and generally requires no treatment, only recognition and reassurance; the rare biallelic neonatal form is severe and demands urgent management.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as primary hyperparathyroidism and performing futile parathyroid surgery
Failing to measure urinary calcium and the clearance ratio before deciding on management
Overlooking a family history of asymptomatic hypercalcaemia
Not recognising that concurrent thiazide or lithium use can confound calcium interpretation
Missing the rare but dangerous neonatal biallelic presentation
